content.text: Dates are ISO and reason codes are clean, so those two can't explain anything. Next I'm checking timing: does wrong-revision scrap come after the new revision arrives, and after the ECO?

input.sql:
WITH s AS (SELECT sr.scrap_id, sr.job_id, sr.reported_on, sr.quantity, j.part_id, j.released_on, j.completed_on, j.revision_issued
 FROM shop_scrap_reports sr JOIN erp_jobs j USING(job_id) WHERE sr.reason_code='wrong revision'),
x AS (SELECT s.*,
 (SELECT min(r.received_on) FROM eng_drawing_revisions r WHERE r.part_id=s.part_id AND r.received_on>s.released_on AND r.received_on<=coalesce(s.completed_on,'9999')) first_mid_rev,
 (SELECT min(r.released_on) FROM eng_drawing_revisions r WHERE r.part_id=s.part_id AND r.received_on>s.released_on AND r.received_on<=coalesce(s.completed_on,'9999')) first_mid_rev_rel,
 (SELECT min(e.logged_on) FROM eng_ecos e WHERE e.job_id=s.job_id) eco_on,
 (SELECT max(r.revision) FROM eng_drawing_revisions r WHERE r.part_id=s.part_id AND r.received_on<=s.reported_on) rev_at_scrap
 FROM s)
SELECT CASE WHEN first_mid_rev IS NULL THEN 'no_mid_rev' WHEN reported_on>=first_mid_rev THEN 'scrap_after_mid_rev_received' ELSE 'scrap_before_mid_rev' END timing,
 CASE WHEN eco_on IS NULL THEN 'no_eco' WHEN eco_on<=reported_on THEN 'eco_before_scrap' ELSE 'eco_after_scrap' END eco_t,
 (rev_at_scrap>revision_issued) newer_rev_existed_at_scrap,
 count(*) n, sum(quantity) q, min(reported_on) mn, max(reported_on) mx
FROM x GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

input.sql:
WITH j AS (
 SELECT j.job_id, j.part_id, j.released_on, j.completed_on, j.revision_issued,
  coalesce((SELECT max(revision) FROM eng_drawing_revisions r WHERE r.part_id=j.part_id AND r.received_on<=j.released_on),'A') rec_rev,
  (SELECT min(r.received_on) FROM eng_drawing_revisions r WHERE r.part_id=j.part_id AND r.received_on>j.released_on AND r.received_on<=coalesce(j.completed_on,'9999')) mid_rec,
  (SELECT min(r.released_on) FROM eng_drawing_revisions r WHERE r.part_id=j.part_id AND r.received_on>j.released_on AND r.received_on<=coalesce(j.completed_on,'9999')) mid_rel,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM eng_ecos e WHERE e.job_id=j.job_id) ecos
 FROM erp_jobs j WHERE j.released_on IS NOT NULL),

WITH j AS (

  (SELECT count(*) FROM eng_drawing_revisions r WHERE r.part_id=j.part_id AND r.received_on>j.released_on AND r.received_on<=coalesce(j.completed_on,'9999')) mid,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM eng_ecos e WHERE e.job_id=j.job_id) ecos
 FROM erp_jobs j JOIN erp_customer_parts p USING(part_id) WHERE j.released_on IS NOT NULL),
m AS (SELECT j.*, (ecos>0) has_eco, job_id IN (SELECT job_id FROM shop_scrap_reports WHERE reason_code='wrong revision') wr FROM j WHERE revision_issued=rec_rev AND mid>0),

content.text:
The finding **stands with changes**: the main pattern got stronger under testing, but the dollar figure should drop from $84,943/yr to **$69,682/yr**. I've saved `challenge.json`.

**What held up:**
- **Not a data artefact.** Dates are stored as `YYYY-MM-DD` text, so comparing them as text gives the right order. The 8 scrap reason codes are clean, with no misspelled variants of "wrong revision" (q376, q377).
- **The timing fits.** All 137 wrong-revision scrap reports were made after a newer revision than the one on the job had been received (q378).
- **The ECO gap survives every split I tried.** Comparing jobs with and without an ECO logged against them, among jobs where a new revision arrived mid-job:
  - It holds when engineering had released the new revision before the job finished: 44.0% of no-ECO jobs had wrong-revision scrap against 0.7% with an ECO. It also holds when the revision was released only after: 31.3% against 0.0%. Job lengths were similar in both groups (q380).
  - It holds within the same customers (40.3% against 0.7%) and within the same parts (48.1% against 1.1%) (q394).
- **An ECO on another job doesn't protect this one.** 49 jobs had no ECO of their own while another job for the same part had one for the same revision; 26 of those 49 still had wrong-revision scrap (q381). That supports checking every open job when a revision arrives.
- **No double counting.** The 81 credit memos ($381,885) each join to one job and reconcile to the other analyst's totals, off by $1 from rounding (q384, q393).

**What changed:**
- **The money basis.** All 137 wrong-revision jobs were scrapped in full, never shipped, and remade (q388). The remake was billed, so the selling price wasn't lost. The real loss is the cost of the scrapped run: material $331,519 plus 2,420 labour hours at the average wage ($60,427). That is 72.0% of the selling-price value. Adding the $304,873 in fit, dimension and nonconforming credits gives **$69,682/yr** over 10 years (q387, q393). The wage has no overheads loaded, so the labour part is understated.
- **Scrap and returns are different jobs.** None of the scrapped jobs has a return; all 81 returns are on jobs that shipped. The finding should describe scrap as problems caught in-house and returns as problems that reached the customer, not as the same events.

**Still uncertain:**
- **The 82 jobs "released on an old revision" depends on the definition.** Using the date engineering logged the revision instead of the date it was received gives 136 (q392). Neither matches the 158 from the earlier query q26, and I couldn't reconcile them.
- **The ECO may not be what prevents the scrap.** Logging an ECO may just record that someone caught the change in time, and that catch is what avoids the scrap. Separating the two would need timestamps on when job packets were updated and a revision check at first-article or final inspection.

**What the finding is not evidence of:**
- That parts were actually made to the wrong drawing. "Wrong revision" is a code entered at the machine, and the revision actually machined isn't recorded.
- That the returns were caused by the revision change. They are on different jobs from the scrap, return reasons are reported by the buyer, and 23 are coded "per buyer".
- Anything about any person's conduct. A missing ECO is a pattern in how changes are recorded.
